newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian rivals jostle in Yeltsin's absence.
newsitem.headline: Russian rivals jostle in Yeltsin's absence.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin's absence as he prepares for heart surgery has provoked more jostling for position within the Kremlin and encouraged speculation that other top politicians are preparing for presidential bids.

The following are brief portraits of the leaders who are likely to be involved in a struggle for power following the decision by doctors on Wednesday to delay Yeltsin's planned heart operation for at least six more weeks.

VIKTOR CHERNOMYRDIN, 58. Prime Minister. Stolid, pro-reform leader who will take over Yeltsin's duties temporarily when the Kremlin leader undergoes surgery. Would assume power for three months until a new election if Yeltsin were incapacitated but has avoided making comments which would make him appear too ambitious. Has been loyal to Yeltsin since he was named prime minister in December 1992 and represents stability for Western economists. Has powerful backers in the natural gas industry which he used to head, and in business circles, but his grey image limits his potential to win votes.

ALEXANDER LEBED, 46. National security adviser and secretary of president's Security Council. Outspoken former paratroop general and Afghan war veteran who was appointed by Yeltsin last June in a vote-winning move after Lebed finished third in presidential election. Has proved independent, unpredictable and outspoken, and won a reputation as a loose cannon by making controversial statements on wide-ranging issues. Main achievement since taking office has been to sign a peace deal in Chechnya but most leaders in Moscow have criticised it. Does not hide presidential ambitions but has little political experience and few allies in the Kremlin, financial circles or other influential groups in Moscow. His views on the economy and reform remain hazy.

YURI LUZHKOV, 60. Moscow Mayor. Won landslide re-election last June which reinforced Muscovites' view of him as a man who gets things done and confirmed his popular appeal. His appeal outside Moscow may be limited but a number of recent trips outside the capital suggest he is trying to widen his appeal and lay the ground for a presidential bid. Backed by big business and financial groups in Moscow, his support would be valuable for any other candidate if he did not run for president and he could become a major powerbroker. Denies he would challenge Yeltsin, with whom he has good relations.

GENNADY ZYUGANOV, 52. Communist Party leader. Was second to Yeltsin in presidential election last July but says he could win if the president stepped down now. He says Russians' patience is wearing thin with the hardships endured under reforms and that frustration with unpaid wages favours him. Has recently forged wider alliance with other leftist and nationalist groups to strengthen the left's bid for power. His presidential ambitions are hampered by limited access to mass media, lack of charisma and few financial resources. Business circles and the West are largely distrustful of his advocacy of a mixed economy of state and private ownership.

ANATOLY CHUBAIS, 41. Head of presidential administration. Unlikely presidential challenger, at least for some years, but widely seen as anxious to consolidate his position. His post as Yeltsin's chief-of-staff gives him huge influence and makes him a potential kingmaker. A former privatisation chief, he is a supporter of rapid reforms who is liked by the West but many workers blame him for the hardships they have endured under reforms. Won high position as reward for helping mastermind Yeltsin's re-election. Widely seen as ally of Chernomyrdin rather than Lebed, he is a fierce critic of Zyuganov and has a bumpy relationship with Luzhkov.
